facts.claim: Acute mountain sickness is a headache with one or more of: loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, fatigue or weakness, dizziness or lightheadedness.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Acute mountain sickness
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Acute mountain sickness

facts.claim: Altitude illness is a risk from about this altitude upwards.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Introduction
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness

facts.claim: The symptoms of acute mountain sickness begin this many hours after arriving at a new altitude, occasionally within the first hour.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Acute mountain sickness

facts.claim: With mild acute mountain sickness, a climber stops going up and rests at the same altitude until the symptoms go; if they get worse, the climber descends.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Treatment of AMS
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Treatment

facts.claim: A climber with symptoms of altitude illness never goes higher.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Treatment

facts.claim: Descending this far usually relieves acute mountain sickness; the climber goes on down until the symptoms go.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Treatment of AMS

facts.claim: High-altitude cerebral edema is the severe end of acute mountain sickness: confusion, drowsiness and ataxia (lost coordination, an unsteady walk), going on to coma.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → High-altitude cerebral edema
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → High-altitude cerebral edema

facts.claim: Ataxia shows when the climber tries to walk heel to toe along a straight line.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → High-altitude cerebral edema

facts.claim: High-altitude cerebral edema requires immediate descent: without it, death can occur within 24 hours of the onset of ataxia.

source.title: CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness

facts.claim: High-altitude pulmonary edema begins as breathlessness on exertion and a fall in performance beyond what altitude explains, then breathlessness at rest and a cough; late on, the lips and nails turn blue and the climber coughs up pink, frothy sputum.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → High-altitude pulmonary edema
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → High-altitude pulmonary edema

facts.claim: High-altitude pulmonary edema usually appears this many days after arriving at a new altitude.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → High-altitude pulmonary edema

facts.claim: High-altitude pulmonary edema can come without any acute mountain sickness before it.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → High-altitude pulmonary edema
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → High-altitude pulmonary edema

facts.claim: High-altitude pulmonary edema is treated by descent, with as little exertion as the climber can manage, since exertion makes it worse; supplemental oxygen enough to bring the blood's oxygen saturation to this level treats it too.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Treatment of HAPE

facts.claim: Descend at once: at any sign of cerebral edema (confusion, drowsiness, ataxia) or of pulmonary edema (breathless at rest), or when acute mountain sickness gets worse in spite of rest at the same altitude.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Treatment
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Treatment

facts.claim: Supplemental oxygen treats acute mountain sickness, cerebral edema and pulmonary edema; where descent isn't possible, it buys time for it.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Treatment

facts.claim: A portable hyperbaric chamber, a bag the sick climber lies in while it is pumped up, simulates a descent: it treats severe illness when descent isn't possible, and the climber still descends afterwards.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Treatment

facts.claim: No medicine replaces a gradual ascent, nor descent once the illness is severe.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Prevention

facts.claim: Acetazolamide speeds up acclimatization: doctors prescribe it to prevent acute mountain sickness and cerebral edema in climbers at moderate or high risk, and to treat acute mountain sickness.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Prevention of AMS and HACE
CDC Yellow Book 2026: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness → Medications

facts.claim: Dexamethasone treats acute mountain sickness and cerebral edema, and can prevent acute mountain sickness, but it doesn't help acclimatization: the symptoms can come back when it stops, so a climber treated with it descends all the same.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Treatment of HACE

facts.claim: Nifedipine lowers the pressure in the arteries of the lungs: doctors prescribe it to prevent pulmonary edema in climbers who have had it before, and to treat it when descent or oxygen isn't possible.

source.title: WMS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Acute Altitude Illness, 2024 Update → Prevention and treatment of HAPE
